name: Ter Saami
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Itkonen, T. I. 1958. Koltan- ja kuolanlapin sanakirja (Ter Saami material); Sammallahti, Pekka. 1998. The Saami Languages: An Introduction.

new_statements.quote: Pääpaino on sanan ensi tavulla. Poikkeuksia on ainoastaan Turjan murteessa, jossa se jakautuu eräissä tapauksissa yhtä suurena ensi ja toiselle tavulle, esim. sanoissa pīrᴅ‘ʌ 'peräsin', kīrᴅ‘ᴇᴅ 'lentää' (arvatenkin ensi tavun ylilyhyyden tähden), pieᴌᴌ‘īᴅ‘ 'poron korvamerkki', oik. pieᴌᴌ‘ᴇ-īᴅ‘ (jossa toisen tavun painollisuus johtunee toisen yhdysosan merkityksen tärkeämmyydestä ensi osan rinnalla). [p. 12:] Yleinen sääntö venäjänlappiin nähden on, että ylin korko on sanan ensi tavulla, kuten pääpainokin. [...] Poikkeuksen tästä tekee kuitenkin turjanlappi, sillä siinä ylin korko siirtyy kolmi- tai useampitavuisissa sanoissa toiselle tavulle, jos tämä on pitkä tai puolipitkä
new_statements.translation: Main stress is on the first syllable of the word. Exceptions occur only in the Turja [= Ter] dialect, where in certain cases it is distributed equally over the first and second syllables, e.g. in the words pīrᴅ‘ʌ 'rudder', kīrᴅ‘ᴇᴅ 'to fly' (presumably because of the over-shortness of the first syllable), pieᴌᴌ‘īᴅ‘ 'reindeer ear-mark', properly pieᴌᴌ‘ᴇ-īᴅ‘ (where the stressedness of the second syllable is probably due to the second member of the compound being semantically more important than the first). [p. 12:] The general rule for Russian Lappish is that the highest pitch is on the first syllable of the word, as is the main stress. [...] Turja Lappish, however, is an exception: there the highest pitch moves, in words of three or more syllables, to the second syllable if that syllable is long or half-long.
new_statements.citation: Itkonen, T. I. 1916. Venäjänlapin konsonanttien astevaihtelu Koltan, Kildinin ja Turjan murteiden mukaan. (Suomalais-Ugrilaisen Seuran Toimituksia 39.) Helsinki: Société Finno-Ougrienne.
new_statements.locator: Section 'Paino', p. 10 (PDF p. 18) and section 'Korko', p. 12 (PDF p. 20); secondary-stress rules p. 11 (PDF p. 19)
new_statements.translation_language: Finnish (FUT transcription of the example words approximated)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level main (expiratory) stress is fixed on the first syllable. In Ter a handful of words show level stress on syllables 1-2 (over-short first syllable, or compounds whose second member is semantically weightier), and the pitch peak in longer words can sit on a long or half-long second syllable, giving Ter its 'singing' intonation. Modern sketches (Kert 1975 for all Kola dialects incl. Jokanga; Agranat's 2023 atlas page for Jokanga) state the rule flatly: main stress always on the first syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Itkonen 1916 p. 11 (stated for Russian Lappish with mostly Skolt examples and one Ter example ḙ̄a·rā:ᴀk‘ 'it freezes'): a long second syllable of a disyllable carries strong secondary stress; in trisyllables secondary stress falls on the last syllable if the second is short, on the second if it is long/half-long and the third short, and on both if both are long; in longer words every long syllable from the second onward carries some secondary stress. Kert 1975 (p. 207, 218) and Agranat (atlas) instead give secondary stress on the odd-numbered syllables except the last.
new_statements.exceptions: Ter-only: equal stress on syllables 1 and 2 in a few words (over-short first syllable; compounds), and highest pitch shifting to a long/half-long second syllable in words of 3+ syllables (Itkonen 1916 pp. 10, 12). Itkonen E. 1946 p. 45 adds that Ter accentuation 'should not differ essentially' from Kildin (main stress syllable 1, strong secondary on syllable 3 in four-syllable words).
new_statements.domain_note: Word stress (tavupaino) as opposed to pitch (korko) and phrase stress; Kert 1975 §14 explicitly restricts the first-syllable rule to isolated words. Itkonen 1916 p. 12 notes that Kildin/Ter phrase stress is monotonous, and that his Jokanga informant's speech had a slow tempo with sentence stress 'almost without rise and fall'.
new_statements.identity_note: Itkonen 1916 calls the language 'Turjan murre' (Turja/Ter dialect of Russian Lappish), with Jokanga informants recorded in 1914; Kert 1961/1975, Tereshkin 2002 and Agranat's atlas call it 'иоканьгский диалект саамского языка' (Jokanga dialect). All map to Glottolog ters1235 (ISO sjt), which has no separate dialect languoids.

sources.note: Sections 'Paino' (pp. 10-11) and 'Korko' (pp. 12-13): main stress on the first syllable in all Russian Lappish; exceptions only in the Turja (=Ter) dialect where a few words carry equal stress on syllables 1 and 2; secondary stress on long non-initial syllables; in Ter the highest pitch shifts to a long/half-long 2nd syllable in words of 3+ syllables. Page images verified (pages16/).

sources.note: Section 4: 'Главное ударение всегда падает на первый слог, второстепенное – на нечетные слоги, кроме последнего.' (Main stress always on the first syllable, secondary on odd syllables except the last.) Survey sketch built on Tereshkin 2002 and Kert; no page numbers.

sources.citation: Kert, G. M. 1975. Saamskij jazyk. In: Osnovy finno-ugorskogo jazykoznanija: Pribaltijsko-finskie, saamskij i mordovskie jazyki, 203-247. Moskva: Nauka.
sources.note: p. 207 (PDF 8, image-verified) lists 'Д. Иоканьгский диалект (поселки Иоканьга, Чальмны-Варрэ)' and states for all Saami dialects: main stress on the first syllable, secondary stresses on odd syllables except the last; §14 'Ударение' p. 218 repeats: bound main stress on syllable 1 (valid for isolated words), secondary on other odd syllables except the last, stresses mechanical and non-distinctive.

Kildin described with main stress on syllable 1 and strong secondary on syllable 3 of four-syllable words (3 1 2 1).
Neither article says anything about stress; the ru bibliography led to the Agranat atlas page.
